full_judgment:
7. As such all the three transferred suits were decreed in favour of the claimant-appellant and against the insurance companies-respondents. 

 12. It is Mr. Ahmed's contention that arbitration in the present case is not a condition precedent to any action on the policy, express words to that effect in Clause 18 notwithstanding. Once the arbitration proceeding draws to a close, the award which will be made the Rule of the Court will have to be executed immediately by the insurers by way of payment of the awarded sum. If, according to Clause 18, the insured has to spend two decades for ascertaining from the arbitrator only the amount of loss or damage sustained by him and has to spend another two decades to obtain a money decree in terms of the award then the insurers' solemn agreement or promise to pay immediately on the happening of the loss becomes a meaningless and illusory statement. Ahmed has referred to a decision in this regard, t which we shall revert later on. 

 22. In the face of an established legal position we are unable to hold that because of considerable passage of time the provision of arbitration in Clause 18 should be treated as a collateral proceeding and should also be interpreted in such a way that irrespective of the insurers reservation on the question of liability, the award itself should be executable and nothing more should be left for the insured to do. If we so hold, an arbitration on a limited point will be converted into a full-fledged decree, which neither the language of Clause 18 nor the long line of established precedents allow us to do. When the law and the contract of insurance both clearly allow the insurers to wait until the amount of loss or damage is settled by the arbitrator, it will be against the principles of justice and fair play and will also be a clear violation of the law of contract and terms and conditions of the policy to saddle them with the liability to pay the loss, even though they have never acknowledged the liability and were within their rights to postpone a decision on liability until the Arbitrator's award is obtained on the quantum of loss or damage.
